23.0.s.en: (1) The failure of the first trial

23.0.1.en: Paul looked intently at these men, among whom he had been a member twenty-five years before, trying Stephen for the same reason for which they were now trying him. Did they know him? And did he know some of them? He called them brethren because he was a member like them in the council of the seventy, and he made clear to them that he had lived serving God with faithfulness when he was a Jew and also after he became a Christian.

23.1.0.en: Ananias: he was the high priest, a Sadducee, unjust and covetous of the portions of the lesser priests, and was greatly hated.

23.1.1.en: Ananias commanded his attendants to strike Paul on the mouth because he showed his sincerity and righteousness, which showed that the members of the council were mistaken in their accusation of him, and this striking meant contempt and mockery of Paul.

23.2.0.en: Paul prophesied about Ananias, saying that God would smite him because he is a hypocritical man, like a wall that is bad inside but whose outside is fair to look at. This prophecy was fulfilled after 5 years, when a rebellion was plotted against him under the leadership of his son, and he fled and hid, but they found him and killed him. Paul rebuked him for commanding that he be struck, as if he were guilty, before his trial, and this is against the law, which gives every person the opportunity to defend himself first.

23.3.0.en: When those near Ananias rebuked him, he said that he did not know that Ananias was the high priest, because the Jews and the Romans used to depose high priests often and appoint others, contrary to the law, which appointed the high priest for all the days of his life.

23.3.1.en: And there was nothing to prove that Ananias was of the descendants of Aaron so as to be high priest. Paul had left the Jewish councils a long time before, so he no longer knew the present high priest, especially since many of those sitting were former high priests, and the high priest had no distinctive clothing outside the service. Paul declared his knowledge of the law (Ex 22:28), which provides that the high priest is not to be reviled; so he was not violating the law, because he did not know that Ananias was high priest.

23.4.0.en: When Paul looked intently at them, he knew that some of them were Pharisees, who believe in spirits and the resurrection, and others were Sadducees, who do not believe in that, but hold that the soul dies with the body and does not rise. So the Holy Spirit guided Paul and he declared that he was of the party of the Pharisees, as was his father, that is, he had lived all his Jewish life as a Pharisee and believes in the resurrection of the dead, which the fathers believe and the Pharisees hold. He said this out of despair of a just judgment of the council upon him, and perhaps by this he might draw the Pharisees to faith in Christ.

23.5.0.en: Although the Sadducees accept the five books of Moses, they do not believe in the resurrection of the dead, nor in the existence of angels, although these are mentioned in those books, for they hold that these angels were created by God for divine purposes in the service of men and then vanished afterward. So when the Pharisees heard that Paul was a Pharisee, they sided with him because he believes as they do against the Sadducees, and here a dissension arose, indeed a dispute, between the two parties over Paul and the accusations directed against him.

23.6.0.en: Most of the scribes were Pharisees and some were Sadducees, and the chief difference between the Pharisees and the Sadducees is belief in the resurrection and immortality. When Paul proclaimed the resurrection of the dead, the Pharisees felt that he was like them, and considered the accusations against him small, so they neglected them and defended him, and regarded the vision which he related to them, of the appearance of Christ to him, as an angel that had appeared to him and called him to preach to the Gentiles. They did not object to that, for what was most important in their view was to oppose the Sadducees, who do not believe in the resurrection.

23.6.1.en: Thus their orators and scribes cried out in defense of Paul. This does not mean that they believed in Christ, but was merely partisanship for their belief in the resurrection against the Sadducees, because they considered Christ merely a spirit or an angel.

23.7.0.en: The commander feared that they would attack Paul and tear him in pieces because of the contention of the two parties to pull him, each to its own side, the Pharisees to protect him and the Sadducees to take vengeance on him, so he commanded the soldiers to take him back to the fortress.

23.8.0.en: The following night, the Lord appeared to Paul to reassure and encourage him, and also to tell him that he would go to preach in Rome according to the desire of his heart. This shows that what Paul said to the high priest was not a fault or anger, but a witness to Christ which He welcomed and encouraged him to continue.

23.8.1.en: The high priest Ananias was a bad example who made people turn away from his religion when they saw him, while Paul, by the purity of his conduct, was a witness to people for his religion. With which of the two parties does each of us stand? Know that your words and actions are noticed by those around you and they follow them. You are the image of Christ; do not turn away from it lest you become a curse to His name, and be confident that example through your behavior is far better than preaching and teaching without practice.

23.9.s.en: (2) The plot and the transfer to Caesarea

23.9.0.en: In the morning, some of the fanatical Jews who were agitated against Paul, of the sect of the Sadducees, agreed together that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.

23.10.0.en: The agitators, who numbered more than forty persons, announced to the chief priests and elders of the Jews their fast from food and drink until they killed Paul. This confirms their insistence on that, and also shows the evil into which the leaders of the Jewish nation had fallen and their determination to kill a man who had not been tried or given an opportunity to defend himself.

23.11.0.en: The agitators were unable to storm the barracks to kill Paul, so they asked the Jewish leaders, who had again agreed on killing Paul after having differed in the council, to request the commander to bring Paul down for his case to be retried and examined, and on the way the agitators would kill him, and thus no charge would be brought against the chief priests.

23.12.0.en: Because the agreement to kill Paul was among a large number, the news leaked to some of the Jews, and the agitators were careful to hide the matter only from the commander, for they did not expect that one of Paul's relatives would be among them, but God permitted Paul's sister's son to be in Jerusalem, and he heard of the plot, so he entered the barracks as a friend of Paul wishing to visit him in the fortress and told him of the matter.

23.13.0.en: Paul sent his sister's son with a centurion to the commander to tell him of the plot, and this shows the importance of a person exerting all his effort for his own salvation, and not relying passively on God's promise of deliverance, as Christ declared to Paul in the vision, that He would deliver him and that he would witness in Rome also.

23.14.0.en: The centurion told the commander that Paul had called him and asked that this young man be brought to the commander to tell him important matters, so the commander was gracious to Paul's sister's son and asked him privately what news he had.

23.15.0.en: The young man told the commander of the plot of the Jews to kill Paul, asking him not to agree to their request to bring Paul down to them.

23.16.0.en: The commander asked him not to tell anyone, lest they take vengeance on him.

23.17.0.en: Caesarea: the seat of the Roman authority in this region, 70 miles from Jerusalem. By the grace of God, the commander believed the young man's words and was concerned to save Paul, so he asked two of his officers to prepare 470 armed soldiers to take Paul to Caesarea at the third hour of the night, that is, nine in the evening by present reckoning, the time when the streets and traffic are quiet.

23.18.0.en: The commander commanded that Paul be mounted and sent under the guard of the soldiers to Felix the Roman at Caesarea.

23.19.0.en: The commander sent a letter to the governor, the text of which St. Luke published.

23.20.0.en: The commander, whose name was Claudius Lysias, sent his greetings to the governor Felix, and informed him that Paul was a Roman by nationality, and that he had rescued him from the hands of the Jews who had seized him, and noticed during his trial before the Jews that the dispute between him and them was religious and not political, and there was no charge against him for which Roman law would hold him accountable.

23.21.0.en: When the commander learned of the plot of the Jews to kill Paul, he hastened to send him to the governor at Caesarea so that the trial might take place there.

23.22.0.en: The soldiers marched all night until they reached the city of Antipatris, having covered two-thirds of the distance to Caesarea.

23.23.0.en: When morning came, the foot soldiers returned to Jerusalem and left with him the horsemen, who completed the road with him to Caesarea, and delivered him and the letter to the governor.

23.24.0.en: The governor inquired of what province Paul was, perhaps to make sure from the records of Cilicia that his citizenship was Roman, or to learn something from his city that would help him regarding the charges against him, or to send him to his city if it was near, to be tried there, if he wished to be rid of him.

23.25.0.en: Felix told Paul that he would hold a lawful trial when his accusers came from Jerusalem, and he kept Paul in custody pending investigation in the great palace of Herod at Caesarea.

23.25.1.en: God's arrangements for the deliverance of His children are very wonderful, for He preserved Paul from evil, and helped him to complete his mission so that he might witness to Christ in Rome. So He works with us when we commit our affairs to Him. Do not be disturbed by the plots of the wicked, for God gives you favor in the eyes of those in authority over you, and delivers you in wonderful ways until you fulfill His will.

23.25.2.en: Paul's continuing as a prisoner until the end of Felix's governorship. Felix had been a slave and was freed, and he was wicked, corrupt and covetous, as will be shown by his later treatment of Paul.

24.0.0.en: After five days Ananias the high priest came with some elders of the Jews, as delegates of the Sanhedrin, and Ananias was full of evil and hatred toward Paul because he had been rebuked by him. He brought with him a Roman advocate named Tertullus, and they began to present their complaint against Paul.

24.1.0.en: They brought Paul for the trial, and the advocate began to plead.

24.2.0.en: Tertullus praised Felix the governor, declaring that the Jewish nation, on whose behalf Tertullus was speaking, enjoyed security because of the justice of his rule, for he had arrested the gangs that committed robbery and murder, and quelled many rebellions, and therefore they thanked him. Although Felix, on the other hand, was characterized by cruelty, injustice and immersion in licentiousness, for he killed Jonathan, the high priest of the Jews, secretly; and the Jews brought a suit against him before the Romans which led to his removal two years after the date of this plea.

24.3.0.en: Tertullus said wisely that he did not wish to expand in describing the virtues of Felix lest he hinder his precious time, and asked humbly that he hear him, as a representative of the Jews, in his clemency. This shows his skill as an orator in persuading and winning the affection of his hearers.

24.4.0.en: The Nazarenes: a contemptuous name for the followers of Christ, since Nazareth was a small town in Galilee, which was full of pagan Gentiles.

24.4.1.en: Tertullus accused Paul of three charges, and considered him a corrupter and harmful to society, and these charges are:

24.4.2.en: 1- That he is a man who corrupts the people and stirs up sedition and discord among all the Jews of the world.

24.4.3.en: 2- That he was not content with creating problems, but led a group which he called the Nazarenes.

24.4.4.en: 3- The third charge with which Tertullus accused Paul was his profaning of the temple by bringing Trophimus the Ephesian, a Gentile, into a place which Gentiles may not enter. This did not happen, but was merely a supposition and claim of the Jews, and the Jews wanted to try him according to the law on these three charges.

24.5.0.en: Tertullus added that the commander Lysias had taken him from them with great violence, and by this he directed blame at the commander for being unjust and said that they had wished to try him justly, while it was they who had been beating Paul with all violence with the intent to kill him.

24.6.0.en: Tertullus continued his speech, accusing the commander Lysias not only of preventing them from trying Paul, but also of burdening them with the hardship of travelling to Caesarea to plead before Felix the governor. And he told the governor that he could make sure of their complaint by questioning the commander and examining Paul, and the Jews agreed to everything Tertullus said.

24.7.0.en: Paul answered, when he was permitted to speak, that he was glad that Felix had governed the Jews for about 6 years, that is, since A.D. 52, because by that he would have come to know the wickedness of the character of the Jews and their cunning.

24.8.0.en: Paul defended himself in two ways:

24.8.1.en: 1- That he had come up to Jerusalem only twelve days before, and had spent most of them in confinement because of the Jews.

24.8.2.en: 2- That he had come to practice worship in the temple as a Jew, for Paul considered Christianity an extension of Judaism and its completion, so he cares for worship in the temple and is not a defiler of it as they accused him.

24.9.0.en: Paul denied their accusation against him that he was a stirrer-up of sedition, as proved by the fact that they had not seized him in the temple disputing or stirring up those present, nor in the synagogues of Jerusalem nor its streets.

24.10.0.en: Paul answered the charge of stirring up sedition and also his profaning of the temple, and showed that they were false charges. As for the third charge, that he was a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes, he declared that he was indeed of the Nazarenes, that is, a Christian, but he made clear that Christianity does not conflict with Judaism but is its completion. For he believes in the God whom the Jews worship, and also believes in the Law and the prophets, and since the Romans recognized Judaism as a religion and Christianity as a sect of it, there was no legal accusation in that.

24.11.0.en: Paul affirmed that as a Christian he believes Judaism, not only in the one God and the Law and the prophets, but he also has hope in the general resurrection like the faith of the Jews. And we notice that the resurrection is for all, righteous and wicked.

24.12.0.en: Paul declared that he strives to have a conscience void of offence before God and to cause no one to stumble.

24.13.0.en: Paul came after his absence from Jerusalem for many years, to offer sacrifices and worship at the feast of Pentecost, and to present alms to the Jews which he had collected from the churches of the Gentiles in which he had preached.

24.14.0.en: The Jews found Paul in the temple with the Asian Jews, that is, the Turks, performing the duties of purification according to the law and offering sacrifices, and they did not find him making a riot; this is his answer to their accusation of him of stirring up sedition. In spite of that, the Jews accused him of having been with Gentiles in the temple, and this of course did not happen. And these Asian Jews, his companions in the temple, did not attend this session of the trial to give their statements and present their complaint if there was anything against him; they are witnesses who could be consulted.

24.15.0.en: The Jews present had tried him in Jerusalem before their council, and had found no fault in him except that he believes in the resurrection of the dead, which the Pharisees supported and the Sadducees objected to.

24.15.1.en: Paul thereby seized the opportunity to preach to those who were trying him and to Felix himself his faith in Christ the Savior who rose from the dead, because Paul's mission as a servant was the most important aim in his life, so he turned every situation into an opportunity for ministry. Would that you seize every opportunity to show Christ through your love and your good conduct and kind words, and do not fear anyone, because God supports you in all the situations of your life.

24.16.0.en: The Jews wanted an immediate judgment from Felix against Paul, but he had some knowledge of Christianity, so he asked them to wait until the commander Lysias came down to Caesarea from Jerusalem and he heard his testimony, because they had cited him in their pleading, and perhaps he was not convinced by their accusations but did not wish to anger them, so he postponed the judgment and left it pending, seeing that Paul was innocent.

24.17.0.en: He commanded the centurion to keep Paul in custody and fix his residence in a specified place without restraints, with permission for him to meet his friends. This shows his conviction of Paul's innocence, but he aimed at pleasing the Jews or at obtaining a bribe from Paul.

24.18.0.en: It seems that Drusilla, Felix's wife, who was a Jewess, asked her husband to see and hear Paul. So he sent for him from his confinement, and he spoke about faith in Christ.

24.19.0.en: Paul spoke about holiness, chastity and the day of judgment, and Felix trembled at that because of his many sins and his fear of judgment, and postponed the rest of the talk to another meeting. And we notice that Drusilla did not tremble at Paul's talk, because she thought that her Judaism and outward religiousness would save her from judgment.

24.20.0.en: Since Felix had heard that Paul had brought with him money for alms for the Christians of Jerusalem, he hoped that Paul would give him a bribe from it to release him, so he repeated his meetings with him, but Paul did not give him any, because of his confidence in his own innocence.

24.21.0.en: Paul remained in custody for two years, until Rome summoned Felix to investigate the complaint of the Jews against him, and Festus came as governor in place of Felix in A.D. 60.

24.21.1.en: And Felix wished to soften his relations with the Jews so that they would withdraw their complaint against him, so he did not release Paul before handing over the governorship to Festus, but left him in his confinement.

24.21.2.en: God turns everything to good for His children. Felix did not know that this action would be the cause of Paul's travelling at the state's expense to Rome, the capital, to be tried there, and to preach in Rome in the name of Christ as he had often wished.

24.21.3.en: So accept God's arrangements even if they are contrary to your will, because God loves you and arranges good for you. Paul before Festus and his appeal to Caesar
